newsitem.title: INDIA: India shares at 34-month high, set for records.
newsitem.headline: India shares at 34-month high, set for records.

text.p: Indian stocks hit a 34-month high on Monday and dealers expected the market to test all-time peaks this week on renewed demand from domestic and foreign funds.
"The main factor is liquidity -- there's so much liquidity in the system," said Mayank Khemka, research head at brokers C. Mackertich & Company.
The benchmark 30-share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) surged to 4,478.19, a new 34-month high, piercing 4,450 for the first time since September 30, 1994.
The index closed up 118.05 points, or 2.72 percent, at 4,465.37. The National exchange index rose 18.0 points to 1,250.40 and the Delhi index added 25.15 points to 973.13.
"The 4,450 was a critical level and now that the market has broken through we can expect a further rise," Khemka said.
Much of the momentum for the rally came from local operators bidding for shares in anticipation of foreign fund demand, players said.
"But still there is not much follow-up foreign fund buying. It's concentrated only in select stocks," said a dealer at a foreign brokerage.
"We expect a correction before the market rallies further."
Last week the index jumped 157.51 points, or 3.76 percent, to 4,347.32.
A sharp rise in index-heavyweight stocks which entered a no-delivery period from Monday also contributed to the index surge, market participants said.
"There is a lot of speculative bidding taking place," said Kamal Kabra, former BSE president and member-broker.
He said much of the action was taking place in smaller capitalised stocks which showed volatile movement on account of the no-delivery period.
The list included Colgate, Steel Authority of India (SAIL), Gujarat Ambuja Cement, Castrol India Ltd, Procter & Gamble, BPL Ltd and Atlas Copco.
A no-delivery period occurs when a company closes its books and market players can buy or sell the company's stock without taking delivery of the shares.
Players get a longer time to close business during the period as against the usual weekly settlement.
Brokers said investor confidence had improved after many companies forecast a revival in business activity in the second half of 1997/98 (April-March).
Last week, engineering and construction giant Larsen & Tourbo and steel major Tata Iron & Steel Company (TISCO) posted improved results in the first quarter ended June 30, 1997.
"The confidence level is improving. It appears that retail interest is coming back into the market," said K.R. Choksey, a member-broker of the BSE.
